subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then score my answer the way an AP reader would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: 1.1 Scalars and Vectors in One Dimension
1.5 Vectors and Motion in Two Dimensions

questions.q: A cart moves along a straight track, with the positive direction to the right. At one instant its acceleration is a_x = −2 m/s². A student claims: "The cart must be slowing down." Which statement correctly evaluates the claim?
options: It is justified: a negative acceleration means that the cart's speed is decreasing with time.
It is not justified: the minus sign tells only that the acceleration points to the left.
It is not justified: the minus sign shows instead that the cart must be moving to the left.
It is not justified: an acceleration cannot be negative, so it is really +2 m/s².
optionWhy: A student who reads a negative acceleration as slowing down picks this. The minus sign gives the direction of the acceleration. If the cart is moving to the left, the same acceleration makes it speed up.

In one dimension the sign of a component gives its direction and nothing else: a_x = −2 m/s² means the acceleration points to the left. The cart slows down if it is moving to the right but speeds up if it is moving to the left, and its velocity is not given.

A student who thinks acceleration points in the direction of motion picks this. The sign of a_x says which way the velocity is changing, not which way the cart moves; the cart could be moving either way.
A student who treats a component as a magnitude picks this. The magnitude of the acceleration, 2 m/s², cannot be negative, but its component a_x can: the minus sign shows that it points to the left.
questions.explain: In one dimension the sign of a component gives its direction and nothing else: a_x = −2 m/s² means the acceleration points to the left. The cart slows down if it is moving to the right but speeds up if it is moving to the left, and its velocity is not given.
questions.working: The sign of a_x gives only the direction of the acceleration (to the left). With v_x > 0 the cart slows down; with v_x < 0 it speeds up. The velocity is not given, so the claim does not follow.

questions.q: The diagram shows arrows representing the velocities of two cars, X and Y, on a straight road at the same instant, drawn to the same scale. The spacing of the grid lines represents 1 m/s. Which claim is supported by the diagram?
options: X is moving twice as fast as Y, in the opposite direction to Y.
X and Y are moving equally fast; the arrows differ only in direction.
Y is moving faster than X, since X points in the negative direction.
X is slowing down, since its velocity points in the negative (−x) direction.
optionWhy: Arrow lengths are proportional to magnitudes. X's arrow spans 4 grid spacings (4 m/s) to the left and Y's spans 2 grid spacings (2 m/s) to the right, so X's speed is twice Y's and the two velocities point in opposite directions.
A student who thinks an arrow's length carries no meaning picks this. In a vector diagram length is proportional to magnitude: X's arrow is twice as long as Y's, so X moves twice as fast.
A student who treats a vector in the negative direction as a smaller quantity picks this. Direction does not affect size: X's arrow is the longer one, so X is the faster car.

A student who reads a velocity in the −x direction as slowing down picks this. A leftward arrow means only that X moves to the left; the diagram shows each car's velocity at one instant and says nothing about whether either speed is changing.
questions.explain: Arrow lengths are proportional to magnitudes. X's arrow spans 4 grid spacings (4 m/s) to the left and Y's spans 2 grid spacings (2 m/s) to the right, so X's speed is twice Y's and the two velocities point in opposite directions.
questions.working: X spans 4 grid spacings to the left: 4 m/s in the −x direction (v_x = −4 m/s). Y spans 2 grid spacings to the right: 2 m/s in the +x direction (v_x = +2 m/s). X's speed is twice Y's, and the directions are opposite.

questions.q: A hiker walks 5 m east and then 9 m west along a straight path. Student 1 takes east as the positive direction; Student 2 takes west as the positive direction. Each finds the hiker's resultant displacement as a signed component. Which statement correctly compares their results?
options: Only Student 1 can be right, as east has to be the positive direction.
Student 1 gets −4 m and Student 2 gets +4 m, and both results mean 4 m west.
Both get +4 m, by subtracting the smaller distance from the larger.
Both get 14 m, since the two walks simply add to give the resultant.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the positive direction is fixed picks this. Either direction may be chosen as positive; Student 2's +4 m, with west positive, describes the same displacement as Student 1's −4 m.

Student 1: +5 m + (−9 m) = −4 m. Student 2: −5 m + (+9 m) = +4 m. The signs differ because the axes differ, but in both coordinate systems the result means 4 m to the west, the same physical displacement.
A student who subtracts magnitudes and drops the sign picks this. With east positive the resultant points west and so is negative, −4 m; only Student 2's axis gives +4 m.

A student who adds the magnitudes of opposite vectors picks this. 14 m is the distance walked. The walks are in opposite directions, so in either coordinate system their components have opposite signs and partly cancel.
questions.explain: Student 1: +5 m + (−9 m) = −4 m. Student 2: −5 m + (+9 m) = +4 m. The signs differ because the axes differ, but in both coordinate systems the result means 4 m to the west, the same physical displacement.
questions.working: East positive: (+5 m) + (−9 m) = −4 m. West positive: (−5 m) + (+9 m) = +4 m. Both mean 4 m west of the starting point.

questions.q: A robot moves along a straight track. It makes displacement A and then displacement B, shown in the diagram drawn tip to tail to scale; the spacing of the grid lines represents 10 m. Taking the positive direction to the right, what is the robot's resultant displacement?
optionWhy: A student who adds the magnitudes, 30 m + 50 m, picks this. That is the distance the robot travels. A and B point in opposite directions, so their components have opposite signs and partly cancel.
A student who subtracts the smaller magnitude from the larger and drops the sign picks this. The larger displacement, B, points to the left, so the resultant points to the left: −20 m, not +20 m.
Give each displacement the sign of its direction and add: A = +30 m and B = −50 m, so the resultant is +30 m + (−50 m) = −20 m. The robot ends 20 m to the left of its starting point.
A student who subtracts instead of adding, B − A = −50 m − 30 m, picks this. That is the difference between the two displacements; the resultant is their sum, A + B.
questions.explain: Give each displacement the sign of its direction and add: A = +30 m and B = −50 m, so the resultant is +30 m + (−50 m) = −20 m. The robot ends 20 m to the left of its starting point.
questions.working: A = +30 m (3 grid spacings to the right); B = −50 m (5 grid spacings to the left). Resultant = (+30 m) + (−50 m) = −20 m, that is, 20 m to the left of the start.

questions.q: A cart moves along a straight track, with the positive direction to the right. At a certain instant the cart's velocity is v_x = −4 m/s. Which statement describes the cart's motion at that instant?
options: It is moving to the right but is slowing down.
It is moving to the left with a speed of −4 m/s.
It is located 4 m to the left of the origin.
It is moving to the left with a speed of 4 m/s.
optionWhy: A student who reads a negative velocity as slowing down picks this. A negative velocity means motion in the negative direction, to the left, and a single velocity value says nothing about whether the speed is changing.
A student who gives the magnitude the component's sign picks this. Speed is a magnitude and is never negative: the cart moves to the left at a speed of 4 m/s.
A student who reads the velocity as a position picks this. v_x = −4 m/s says which way and how fast the cart moves, not where it is; the cart could be anywhere on the track.
The minus sign gives the direction: the cart moves in the negative direction, to the left. The magnitude, 4 m/s, is its speed.
questions.explain: The minus sign gives the direction: the cart moves in the negative direction, to the left. The magnitude, 4 m/s, is its speed.
questions.working: The sign gives the direction (negative: to the left); the magnitude, 4 m/s, is the speed.

questions.q: The diagram shows the velocities of four carts, P, Q, R and S, moving along straight tracks, at t = 0 and at t = 2.0 s. The positive direction is to the right, and each arrow is labeled with its speed. Which cart has the greatest magnitude of average acceleration between t = 0 and t = 2.0 s?
options: Cart P
Cart Q
Cart R
Cart S
optionWhy: Average acceleration is Δv/Δt, using signed velocities. This cart goes from +3 m/s to −3 m/s, so Δv = −6 m/s and the magnitude of its average acceleration is 6 m/s ÷ 2.0 s = 3.0 m/s², the largest of the four (the others are 2.0, 2.5 and 0 m/s²).

A student who thinks only speeding up counts as accelerating picks this, the one cart that speeds up. Its velocity changes by 4 m/s, an average acceleration of 2.0 m/s²; the cart that reverses has a larger change of velocity, 6 m/s.

A student who uses the change in speed picks this: its speed falls by 5 m/s, more than any other cart's. But the cart that reverses changes its velocity by 6 m/s, from +3 m/s to −3 m/s, even though its speed ends where it began.
A student who links a greater speed with a greater acceleration picks this, the fastest cart. Its velocity is the same at both times, so its average acceleration is zero.
questions.explain: Average acceleration is Δv/Δt, using signed velocities. This cart goes from +3 m/s to −3 m/s, so Δv = −6 m/s and the magnitude of its average acceleration is 6 m/s ÷ 2.0 s = 3.0 m/s², the largest of the four (the others are 2.0, 2.5 and 0 m/s²).
questions.working: Δt = 2.0 s. P: +3 m/s → −3 m/s, Δv = −6 m/s, |a_avg| = 3.0 m/s²; Q: +2 m/s → +6 m/s, Δv = +4 m/s, |a_avg| = 2.0 m/s²; R: +6 m/s → +1 m/s, Δv = −5 m/s, |a_avg| = 2.5 m/s²; S: +7 m/s → +7 m/s, Δv = 0 m/s, |a_avg| = 0.0 m/s². Greatest magnitude: cart P.

questions.q: A ball moving at 5.0 m/s toward a wall bounces straight back at 5.0 m/s. A student claims that the ball does not accelerate during the bounce. Which statement correctly evaluates the claim?
options: Correct: the ball's speed after the bounce is the same as its speed before it.
Correct: the ball comes to rest during the bounce, and a ball at rest has no acceleration.
Incorrect: it accelerates as it speeds back up, but not while it slows down.
Incorrect: the direction of the ball's velocity changes, so the ball accelerates.
optionWhy: A student who judges acceleration by the change in speed alone picks this. Velocity includes direction, and reversing it is a change in velocity, so the ball accelerates.

A student who thinks an object at rest cannot be accelerating picks this. At the instant the ball is at rest its velocity is changing from toward the wall to away from it, so its acceleration is not zero, and the ball accelerates throughout the bounce.
A student who thinks 'accelerating' means only speeding up picks this. While the ball slows down against the wall its velocity is changing too, so it is accelerating then as well.

An object accelerates if the magnitude or the direction of its velocity changes. The speed is the same before and after, but the velocity reverses, from 5.0 m/s toward the wall to 5.0 m/s away from it: a change of 10 m/s directed away from the wall.
questions.explain: An object accelerates if the magnitude or the direction of its velocity changes. The speed is the same before and after, but the velocity reverses, from 5.0 m/s toward the wall to 5.0 m/s away from it: a change of 10 m/s directed away from the wall.

questions.q: Cart A speeds up from 2.0 m/s to 8.0 m/s in 3.0 s. Cart B speeds up from 24.0 m/s to 28.0 m/s in 2.0 s. Both carts move in the +x direction along straight tracks. Which statement correctly compares the magnitudes of their average accelerations?
options: They are equal, since each cart's velocity changes by 2.0 m/s per second on average.
B's is greater, since cart B is moving much faster than cart A throughout.
A's is greater, since A's velocity changes by 6.0 m/s but B's by only 4.0 m/s.
B's is greater, since B's final velocity divided by its time is the larger value.
optionWhy: a_avg = Δv/Δt. Cart A: 6.0 m/s ÷ 3.0 s = 2.0 m/s². Cart B: 4.0 m/s ÷ 2.0 s = 2.0 m/s². The average accelerations are equal.
A student who links a greater speed with a greater acceleration picks this. Acceleration depends on how quickly the velocity changes, not on how large it is; both average accelerations are 2.0 m/s².
A student who equates acceleration with the change in velocity picks this. A's larger change takes longer: 6.0 m/s in 3.0 s and 4.0 m/s in 2.0 s are both 2.0 m/s².
A student who divides the final velocity by the time picks this (28.0 ÷ 2.0 for B, 8.0 ÷ 3.0 for A). Neither cart started from rest, so the change in velocity must be used.
questions.explain: a_avg = Δv/Δt. Cart A: 6.0 m/s ÷ 3.0 s = 2.0 m/s². Cart B: 4.0 m/s ÷ 2.0 s = 2.0 m/s². The average accelerations are equal.
questions.working: a_A = (8.0 − 2.0) m/s ÷ 3.0 s = 2.0 m/s². a_B = (28.0 − 24.0) m/s ÷ 2.0 s = 2.0 m/s². They are equal. (Final velocity ÷ time would give 2.7 m/s² for A and 14 m/s² for B.)

questions.q: A cyclist rides in a straight line in the +x direction. She covers the first half of the total distance D at a constant speed v and the second half at a constant speed 2v. Which expression gives the magnitude of her average velocity for the whole ride?
optionWhy: A student who averages the two speeds, (v + 2v)/2, picks this. The halves do not last equal times (the slower half takes twice as long), so the simple mean gives the faster half too much weight; divide the total displacement by the total time instead.
A student who divides the time interval by the displacement, (3D/(4v)) ÷ D, picks this. It has units s/m, not m/s; average velocity is Δx/Δt.

A student who divides the displacement of one half, D/2, by the time for the whole ride, 3D/(4v), picks this. The displacement and the time interval must describe the same interval: over the whole ride, Δx = D.

The two halves take different times: D/(2v) at speed v and D/(4v) at speed 2v, so Δt = 3D/(4v). The average velocity uses the initial and final states of the whole interval: Δx/Δt = D ÷ (3D/(4v)) = (4/3)v. It is nearer v than 2v because the slower half lasts twice as long.
questions.explain: The two halves take different times: D/(2v) at speed v and D/(4v) at speed 2v, so Δt = 3D/(4v). The average velocity uses the initial and final states of the whole interval: Δx/Δt = D ÷ (3D/(4v)) = (4/3)v. It is nearer v than 2v because the slower half lasts twice as long.
questions.working: First half: t_1 = (D/2)/v = D/(2v). Second half: t_2 = (D/2)/(2v) = D/(4v). Whole ride: Δt = t_1 + t_2 = 3D/(4v). She rides in one direction only, so Δx = +D. v_avg = Δx/Δt = D ÷ (3D/(4v)) = (4/3)v. (Mean of the two speeds: (v + 2v)/2 = (3/2)v. Time divided by displacement: (3D/(4v)) ÷ D = 3/(4v), units s/m. Displacement of one half over the whole time: (D/2) ÷ (3D/(4v)) = (2/3)v.) The slower half lasts twice as long as the faster half, so the average lies nearer v than 2v.

questions.q: The graph shows the velocity v of a car as a function of time t as the car pulls away from rest along a straight, level road. Which statement describes the car's motion during the time shown?
options: Its speed rises to a steady value as its acceleration decreases to zero.
Its speed and its acceleration both increase during the time shown.
It slows down, since its acceleration decreases as time goes on.
It comes to rest at the instant when the graph becomes a horizontal line.
optionWhy: The velocity (height) rises and then levels off, so the speed increases to a steady value. The slope, which is the acceleration, is greatest at the start and decreases to zero where the graph becomes horizontal.

A student who links the size of the acceleration to the speed picks this. The speed does increase, but the slope of the graph decreases: the car gains speed ever more slowly, so its acceleration decreases.

A student who thinks a decreasing acceleration means slowing down picks this. The acceleration does decrease, but it stays in the direction of motion until it reaches zero, so the car keeps speeding up; the velocity never falls.

A student who reads a level line as 'not moving', as on a position–time graph, picks this. On a velocity–time graph a level line well above the time axis means a constant, nonzero velocity: the car keeps moving at a steady speed.
questions.explain: The velocity (height) rises and then levels off, so the speed increases to a steady value. The slope, which is the acceleration, is greatest at the start and decreases to zero where the graph becomes horizontal.

figure.alt: Velocity–time graph with v (m/s) on the vertical axis and t (s) on the horizontal axis; no values are marked except 0 at the origin. The curve starts at the origin, rises steeply at first, becomes gradually less steep, and ends as a horizontal line well above the time axis.

questions.q: The graph shows the velocity v of an object moving along a straight line as a function of time t. A student claims that the object's acceleration is zero at t = 3 s, because the object is at rest at that instant. Which statement correctly evaluates the claim?
options: Correct: the velocity is zero at t = 3 s, so the velocity is not changing then.
Incorrect: the acceleration changes from positive to negative at the instant t = 3 s.
Incorrect: the graph has the same slope at t = 3 s as at every other time.
Incorrect: the acceleration is negative before t = 3 s and positive after it.
optionWhy: A student who thinks zero velocity means zero acceleration picks this. The velocity is zero at t = 3 s, but it is changing: it goes from positive just before 3 s to negative just after, at a steady −4 m/s².

A student who thinks acceleration points in the direction of motion picks this, because the object moves in the positive direction before 3 s and the negative direction after. The slope, and so the acceleration, is negative throughout.

Acceleration is the slope of the velocity–time graph. The graph is one straight line, so its slope, (−4 − 12) m/s ÷ 4 s = −4 m/s², is the same at every instant, including t = 3 s where the velocity passes through zero.

A student who thinks a positive acceleration means speeding up picks this, because the object slows before 3 s and speeds up after. After 3 s it speeds up in the negative direction; the slope is still negative, so the acceleration is still −4 m/s².
questions.explain: Acceleration is the slope of the velocity–time graph. The graph is one straight line, so its slope, (−4 − 12) m/s ÷ 4 s = −4 m/s², is the same at every instant, including t = 3 s where the velocity passes through zero.
questions.working: Slope = (−4 − 12) m/s ÷ (4 − 0) s = −4 m/s² at every instant. v = 12 − 4t = 0 at t = 3 s. So a = −4 m/s² at t = 3 s: the claim is incorrect.

questions.q: The graph shows the position x of an object moving along a straight line as a function of time t. Points A, B and C are on the curve; the curve is horizontal at B. Which ranks the object's speeds at A, B and C, from greatest to least?
options: B > C > A
A > C > B
A > B > C
B > A > C
optionWhy: A student who ranks the heights of the points (8 m, 6 m, 1.5 m) picks this. The height of a position–time graph is the position; B is the farthest point from the origin, but the curve is flat there, so the object is momentarily at rest.

Speed is the size of the slope of the tangent to the position–time graph. The curve is steepest at A (a slope of about 3 m/s), less steep at C (sloping down, about 1.5 m/s), and horizontal at B (zero), so A > C > B.

A student who ranks the signed velocities picks this: positive at A, zero at B, negative at C. The question asks for speeds, the magnitudes of the slopes; the object moves faster at C (in the negative direction) than at B, where it is at rest.

A student who takes x/t at each point as the speed (1.5 m/s at A, 2.0 m/s at B, about 0.9 m/s at C) picks this. x/t is the slope of a line from the origin, an average velocity; the speed at an instant is the slope of the tangent, which is zero at B.
questions.explain: Speed is the size of the slope of the tangent to the position–time graph. The curve is steepest at A (a slope of about 3 m/s), less steep at C (sloping down, about 1.5 m/s), and horizontal at B (zero), so A > C > B.
questions.working: Tangent slopes: A about +3 m/s (steep, rising), B 0 (horizontal), C about −1.5 m/s (falling, less steep than at A). Speeds: A ≈ 3 m/s > C ≈ 1.5 m/s > B = 0.

questions.q: The graph shows the velocity v of an object moving along a straight line as a function of time t. Which statement about the object's motion from t = 0 to t = 4 s is correct?
options: Its position is least at t = 2 s, the instant when its velocity is zero.
Its position is least at t = 0, the instant when its velocity is most negative.
Its speed increases throughout, since its acceleration is positive.
Its acceleration is zero at t = 2 s, the instant when its velocity is zero.
optionWhy: From 0 to 2 s the velocity is negative, so the object moves in the negative direction and its position decreases. After 2 s the velocity is positive and the position increases. The position is therefore least at t = 2 s, when the object reverses.

A student who reads the height of the velocity graph as the position picks this. At t = 0 the object is moving in the negative direction, so its position is still decreasing; it keeps decreasing until the velocity reaches zero at t = 2 s.

A student who thinks a positive acceleration always means speeding up picks this. From 0 to 2 s the velocity is negative and the acceleration positive, so the object slows down (its speed falls from 4 m/s to 0); it speeds up only after 2 s.
A student who thinks zero velocity means zero acceleration picks this. The graph is a straight line with the same slope, +2 m/s², at t = 2 s as at every other time; only the velocity is zero there.
questions.explain: From 0 to 2 s the velocity is negative, so the object moves in the negative direction and its position decreases. After 2 s the velocity is positive and the position increases. The position is therefore least at t = 2 s, when the object reverses.
questions.working: Slope = (4 − (−4)) m/s ÷ 4 s = +2 m/s², constant. v < 0 for 0 < t < 2 s (moving in −x, position decreasing, slowing), v = 0 at t = 2 s, v > 0 afterwards (moving in +x, speeding up). Displacement 0–2 s = −4 m, 2–4 s = +4 m, so x is least at t = 2 s.

questions.q: A cart moves along a straight track, speeding up relative to the track. Observer G stands beside the track. Observer R rides on a platform that moves along the track at constant velocity. The table shows the cart's velocity v measured by each observer at four instants t. Which claim is supported by the data?
options: R finds that the cart's acceleration reverses at t = 2.0 s.
R finds the same acceleration for the cart as G, 2.0 m/s².
R finds a smaller acceleration, since R moves the same way as the cart.
R finds zero acceleration at t = 2.0 s, when it sees the cart at rest.
optionWhy: A student who treats acceleration as the rate of change of speed picks this. R sees the speed fall from 4.0 m/s to 0 and then rise, but R's signed velocity increases by 2.0 m/s every second, so R's measured acceleration is constant and positive throughout.

Each observer's velocity rises by 2.0 m/s in each 1.0 s interval: G from 1.0 m/s to 7.0 m/s and R from −4.0 m/s to 2.0 m/s over 3.0 s. Both measure 6.0 m/s ÷ 3.0 s = 2.0 m/s². R's values are all 5.0 m/s lower, a constant shift that leaves every change in velocity unchanged.

A student who thinks acceleration changes from frame to frame like velocity picks this. R's velocities are smaller, but they change by the same 2.0 m/s each second as G's, so R's acceleration is the same.

A student who thinks zero velocity means zero acceleration picks this. R's velocity passes through zero at 2.0 s but goes from −2.0 m/s to 0 to 2.0 m/s in equal times, so the acceleration there is still 2.0 m/s².
questions.explain: Each observer's velocity rises by 2.0 m/s in each 1.0 s interval: G from 1.0 m/s to 7.0 m/s and R from −4.0 m/s to 2.0 m/s over 3.0 s. Both measure 6.0 m/s ÷ 3.0 s = 2.0 m/s². R's values are all 5.0 m/s lower, a constant shift that leaves every change in velocity unchanged.
questions.working: G: Δv = 7.0 − 1.0 = 6.0 m/s in 3.0 s, a = 2.0 m/s²; each second +2.0 m/s. R: Δv = 2.0 − (−4.0) = 6.0 m/s in 3.0 s, a = 2.0 m/s²; each second +2.0 m/s. Every R value is the G value minus 5.0 m/s, so R moves at +5.0 m/s. Same acceleration, constant, positive throughout.

questions.q: A cyclist rides east at 6 m/s relative to the road. Observer X stands beside the road. Observer Y is in a car that moves east along the same road at a constant 10 m/s. Which statement correctly compares the cyclist's velocity as measured by Y with the velocity measured by X?
options: Y measures the same velocity as X does, 6 m/s east along the road.
Y measures a smaller speed than X does, and in the opposite direction.
Y measures a larger speed than X does, and in the same direction.
Y measures a smaller speed than X does, in the same direction.
optionWhy: A student who takes the ground-frame velocity as the one every observer reports picks this. Y moves, so Y's measurement must include Y's own velocity: 6 m/s − 10 m/s = −4 m/s.

Y measures the cyclist's velocity minus Y's own velocity: 6 m/s − 10 m/s = −4 m/s, so 4 m/s west. The car pulls ahead of the cyclist, so from the car the cyclist drops back (moves west) at 4 m/s, a smaller speed than the 6 m/s that X measures.

A student who adds the observer's velocity instead of subtracting it picks this, getting 6 m/s + 10 m/s = 16 m/s east. An observer moving the same way as the cyclist must see the cyclist move more slowly, not faster.

A student who subtracts in the wrong order, 10 m/s − 6 m/s = +4 m/s, picks this. That is Y's velocity relative to the cyclist. The car is faster, so relative to the car the cyclist moves backward, to the west.
questions.explain: Y measures the cyclist's velocity minus Y's own velocity: 6 m/s − 10 m/s = −4 m/s, so 4 m/s west. The car pulls ahead of the cyclist, so from the car the cyclist drops back (moves west) at 4 m/s, a smaller speed than the 6 m/s that X measures.
questions.working: East positive, ground frame. X: +6 m/s. Y: v_cyclist − v_Y = 6 − 10 = −4 m/s, i.e. 4 m/s west: a smaller speed than X measures (4 < 6) and the opposite direction.

questions.q: Car A and truck B move along a straight road. The graph shows their positions x as functions of time t, measured by an observer standing beside the road. What is the velocity of truck B as measured by the driver of car A?
optionWhy: The slopes give the ground-frame velocities: v_A = 100 m ÷ 4 s = +25 m/s and v_B = −60 m ÷ 4 s = −15 m/s. The driver of A measures v_B − v_A = −15 m/s − 25 m/s = −40 m/s: the vehicles approach each other, so their relative speed is the sum of their speeds.
A student who subtracts in the wrong order, v_A − v_B, picks this. That is A's velocity measured by the truck driver. From car A the truck approaches from ahead, moving in the −x direction.

A student who drops the signs and takes the difference of the speeds, 25 m/s − 15 m/s, picks this. The vehicles move in opposite directions, so with signed velocities the relative velocity is −15 m/s − (+25 m/s) = −40 m/s: the truck approaches car A at 40 m/s.
A student who reports the truck's velocity relative to the road picks this. That is what the roadside observer measures; the driver of A moves at +25 m/s, and that velocity must be subtracted.
questions.explain: The slopes give the ground-frame velocities: v_A = 100 m ÷ 4 s = +25 m/s and v_B = −60 m ÷ 4 s = −15 m/s. The driver of A measures v_B − v_A = −15 m/s − 25 m/s = −40 m/s: the vehicles approach each other, so their relative speed is the sum of their speeds.
questions.working: Slopes (ground frame): v_A = (100 m − 0)/(4 s) = +25 m/s; v_B = (140 m − 200 m)/(4 s) = −15 m/s. Velocity of B relative to A: v_B − v_A = −15 m/s − 25 m/s = −40 m/s.

questions.q: A ball is launched horizontally with speed v_x0 from the edge of a cliff of height h above level ground. Air resistance is negligible. Just before the ball lands, its velocity makes an angle φ below the horizontal. Which expression gives tan φ?
options: √(gh)/v_x0
2gh/v_x0
optionWhy: Horizontally, v_x = v_x0 throughout. Vertically, the ball falls h from rest, so v_y² = 2gh and |v_y| = √(2gh) at landing. The components are perpendicular, so tan φ = |v_y|/v_x = √(2gh)/v_x0.
A student who uses h = gt², without the factor 1/2, gets t = √(h/g) and |v_y| = gt = √(gh), and picks this. For a fall from rest, h = (1/2)gt², so t = √(2h/g) and |v_y| = √(2gh).

A student who writes v_y² = 2gh and then uses 2gh as v_y, without taking the square root, picks this. The expression is not even a ratio of two speeds: 2gh has units m²/s². Take the square root: |v_y| = √(2gh).

A student who takes the velocity to point along the straight line from the launch point to the landing point uses tan φ = h/R, with R = v_x0√(2h/g), and picks this. The velocity is tangent to the path, not along the displacement; its direction comes from its components, and its tangent is twice as large.
questions.explain: Horizontally, v_x = v_x0 throughout. Vertically, the ball falls h from rest, so v_y² = 2gh and |v_y| = √(2gh) at landing. The components are perpendicular, so tan φ = |v_y|/v_x = √(2gh)/v_x0.
questions.working: Separate the motion into components. Vertical: the ball starts with v_y0 = 0 and falls a height h with acceleration of magnitude g, so v_y² = v_y0² + 2gh = 2gh and |v_y| = √(2gh) at landing. Horizontal: no acceleration, so v_x = v_x0 throughout. The components are perpendicular, so tan φ = |v_y|/v_x = √(2gh)/v_x0. (Using h = gt² instead of h = (1/2)gt²: t = √(h/g), |v_y| = gt = √(gh). Omitting the square root in v_y² = 2gh: 2gh/v_x0, which has units m/s and so cannot be a tangent. Along the straight line from launch point to landing point: tan = h/R with R = v_x0√(2h/g), which is √(gh/2)/v_x0, half the key.)

questions.q: A ball is launched into the air. The horizontal and vertical components of its velocity, v_x and v_y, are shown as functions of time t in the graphs, with upward positive. Air resistance is negligible. Which claim about the ball's motion is supported by the graphs?
options: It is momentarily at rest at t = 2 s, where v_y is zero.
Its speed is least at t = 2 s, where it equals 6 m/s.
Its speed at t = 0 is 26 m/s, the sum of 6 m/s and 20 m/s.
Its acceleration is zero at t = 2 s, where v_y is zero.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a projectile stops at its highest point picks this. At t = 2 s only v_y is zero; the upper graph shows v_x = 6 m/s at that time, so the ball is moving horizontally.
The speed is √(v_x² + v_y²). v_x is 6 m/s throughout, and v_y is zero at t = 2 s and larger in size at every other time, so the speed is least at 2 s, where it is just v_x = 6 m/s.
A student who adds the component magnitudes as ordinary numbers picks this. Perpendicular components combine by the Pythagorean relationship: √((6 m/s)² + (20 m/s)²) ≈ 21 m/s.
A student who thinks the acceleration is zero at the highest point picks this. The v_y graph is a straight line with slope −40 m/s ÷ 4 s = −10 m/s² at every time, including t = 2 s.
questions.explain: The speed is √(v_x² + v_y²). v_x is 6 m/s throughout, and v_y is zero at t = 2 s and larger in size at every other time, so the speed is least at 2 s, where it is just v_x = 6 m/s.
questions.working: v_x = 6 m/s constant; v_y = 20 − 10t (m/s), zero at t = 2 s. Speed = √(6² + v_y²): at t = 0 it is √(36 + 400) = 20.9 m/s; least at t = 2 s, where it is 6 m/s. Slope of v_y–t = −40/4 = −10 m/s² at every time, including t = 2 s.

questions.q: The diagram shows the path of a ball launched from level ground and moving from left to right. Air resistance is negligible. Points P and R are at the same height, and Q is the highest point of the path. Which ranking of the horizontal component of the ball's velocity, v_x, at the three points is correct?
options: P > Q > R
P = R > Q
Q > P = R
P = Q = R
optionWhy: A student who thinks the ball's forward motion is gradually used up picks this. With air resistance negligible nothing acts horizontally on the ball, so v_x stays constant along the whole path.
A student who thinks the ball stops at the highest point picks this. At Q only the vertical component is zero; the ball is still moving sideways with the same v_x as at P and R.

A student who thinks the speed stays the same and becomes all horizontal at the top picks this. The speed is actually least at Q; v_x is the same at all three points, and at Q it is simply the whole velocity.

A projectile's acceleration is vertical (g downward), so its horizontal acceleration is zero and v_x never changes: it has the same value at P, at Q and at R. Only the vertical component changes along the path.
questions.explain: A projectile's acceleration is vertical (g downward), so its horizontal acceleration is zero and v_x never changes: it has the same value at P, at Q and at R. Only the vertical component changes along the path.
questions.working: Projectile: a_x = 0, so v_x is constant: v_x(P) = v_x(Q) = v_x(R). (Speed ranking would be P = R > Q, because v_y = 0 at Q.)

questions.q: A ball is launched horizontally from the top of a wall and lands a horizontal distance d from the base of the wall. Air resistance is negligible. The ball is then launched with the same horizontal speed from the top of a wall twice as high. The new horizontal distance is approximately how many times d?
optionWhy: A student who reasons that the horizontal motion is independent of the vertical, so the height cannot matter, picks this. The two motions share the same time, and a higher launch gives a longer time of fall.

A student who treats the time of fall as proportional to the height, as if t = 2h/g without the square root, picks this. t is proportional to √h, so doubling h multiplies the time, and the distance, by √2.

The time of fall comes from the vertical motion: h = (1/2)g t², so t = √(2h/g) is proportional to √h. The horizontal distance is v_x0 t, also proportional to √h. Doubling the height multiplies the distance by √2 ≈ 1.4.
A student who inverts h = (1/2)g t² as if t were proportional to h² picks this. The square belongs to t: t² ∝ h, so t ∝ √h.
questions.explain: The time of fall comes from the vertical motion: h = (1/2)g t², so t = √(2h/g) is proportional to √h. The horizontal distance is v_x0 t, also proportional to √h. Doubling the height multiplies the distance by √2 ≈ 1.4.
questions.working: Vertical: h = (1/2)g t², so t = √(2h/g) ∝ √h. Horizontal: x = v_x0 t ∝ √h. Height × 2 → t × √2 → distance × √2 ≈ 1.4.
